sharedText: came also in the days of
reason: A six-word run and one of the chapter's highest-scoring candidates, and it is pure dating formula on both sides. Jeremiah 1:3 is a superscription fixing a prophet's ministry to two reigns; Ether 11:1 is the abridger's standing way of attaching an episode to a king, used again at 11:12 ('in the days of Ethem') and 11:20 ('in the days of Coriantor') and throughout Ether 6-10. A formula the Book of Mormon uses continuously cannot be a borrowing from the one KJV verse that happens to share its wording. This entry covers the 'in the days of X' candidates at 11:7, 11:12 and 11:20 as well; they are not listed individually.

Four words of narrative connective tissue introducing an arrival. John 19:39's arrival is Nicodemus with the myrrh and aloes for the burial of Jesus; Ether 11:1's is a body of prophets. Nothing but the verb and its adverb is shared, and the real link at this verse is to Acts 26:20 later in the same sentence.

sharedText: (prophets sheltered from a régime that is killing them)
reason: Written up at length because a reader who knows the Elijah cycle will see it here and should be told the catalogue saw it too. Ether 11:2 has prophets who cannot stay among a people that wants them dead and who are taken in by a man with power; 1 Kings 18:4 has Obadiah hiding a hundred prophets by fifty in a cave and feeding them with bread and water while Jezebel cuts off the prophets of the LORD — and Ether 11:5, three verses later, has a royal brother who 'did cause that all the prophets which prophesied of the destruction of the people, should be put to death', which is Jezebel's act exactly. Jeremiah 26 offers the same shape with a closer legal setting: the people demand Jeremiah's death (26:8-11), Urijah the prophet actually is executed (26:20-23), and Ahikam's hand is with Jeremiah 'that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death' (26:24). The wording will not bear either. 1 Kings 18:4 shares no distinctive string with Ether 11:2, and Jeremiah 26:24's 'into the hand of the people' is not what Ether says. The verbal source at this verse is Luke 19:47, where 'the people sought to destroy' is a KJV singleton, and the Elijah and Jeremiah material is a type the chapter conforms to rather than a text it quotes.

Four words of inceptive auxiliary. Genesis 9:20's continuation is 'husbandman' and Ether 11:4's is 'exceeding great war'; the shared material is a tense, not a phrase. 'There began to be' is among the Book of Mormon's most frequent constructions and is covered by the standing exclusion on connective boilerplate.

The best refusal in this chapter's register, because the rarity is genuine and would tempt anyone: “a great curse” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 23:14. The senses are not merely different, they are structurally opposed. In Acts the curse is an oath men bind upon themselves — forty conspirators swearing to eat nothing until they have murdered Paul — so the curse is an instrument of the killing and its subject is the killers by their own choice. In Ether 11:6 the curse is a sentence pronounced from outside upon a land and its inhabitants, testified by the prophets the people are about to kill, and its subject is the killers against their will. Acts' curse is a means; Ether's is a consequence. Nothing else of Acts 23 is present, and the surrounding material at 11:6 comes from Daniel 12:1 and Jeremiah 8:1-2. Worth noting for the record that the chapter does borrow from Acts elsewhere — 11:1 takes Acts 26:20 — which makes the coincidence here more tempting and no more real.

A five-word run of inceptive boilerplate whose completions are opposite in every respect: Numbers 25:1 continues 'to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab' and Ether 11:8 continues 'to repent of their iniquity'. The Israelite apostasy at Shittim has no other contact with this verse. Where Ether 11:8 does have a source it is Judges 2:18, adjudicated as part of the Judges 2 row at 11:13.

Four words of subordinating connective. Numbers 11:29 is Moses wishing all the LORD's people were prophets; Ether 11:12 is prophets announcing an extermination. The real contact at this verse is 'utterly destroy them from off the face of the earth', adjudicated to Amos 9:8.

A genuine candidate and a close one — Ezekiel 20:8's 'they rebelled against me, and would not hearken unto me' shares four words and the sense — but it is superseded. Ether 11:13 reads 'would not hearken unto their words', and “would not hearken unto their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:17, where the object is 'their judges'. Ether has the possessive construction Ezekiel lacks. The Judges 2 reading also explains the neighbouring verses, which Ezekiel 20 does not: 11:8's relenting mercy is Judges 2:18 and the chapter's each-reign-worse-than-the-last movement is Judges 2:19. See the link at 11:13.

“reign in his stead” is a KJV singleton in that exact form only because the King James Bible almost always writes the past tense; “reigned in his stead” occurs in sixty-three verses and 'in his stead' in seventy-three. It is the regnal-annals formula of Kings and Chronicles, and the Book of Mormon has been using it since Ether 7:3 — 8:1, 9:22, 9:25, 10:18 and again here. A formula that recurs continuously through a book cannot be a borrowing from any single verse of the source it is imitating wholesale. Solomon's speech at Gibeon has no other contact with Ether 11:14. The same reason covers the 'all his days' and 'begat' candidates through 11:9-19.

“there arose a mighty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the next word decides everything: Luke's is 'famine' and Ether's is 'man'. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names — the window closing one word early — in its purest form, because the shared four words are a complete grammatical unit and the divergence is entirely in the noun. Luke 15:14 is the turn of the prodigal parable, a famine in a far country reducing a son to want; Ether 11:15 is a usurper rising out of a secret combination to take half a kingdom by battle. Recorded because the run is long and the ranking high, and because 'a mighty famine' and 'a mighty man' will keep re-proposing themselves to any n-gram stream.

“a mighty man” occurs in seventeen KJV verses and is the Bible's standing epithet for a warrior; 1 Chronicles 12:4's Ismaiah the Gibeonite is a name in a muster roll of David's men at Ziklag. Ether 11:15's man is anonymous, rises 'in iniquity' out of a secret combination, and fights the king. The three shared words are an epithet plus a preposition, distributed across the historical books, and they point at no verse in particular.

Five words of connective. John 9:16's division among the people is a dispute over whether a sabbath healer is of God; Ether 11:15's is an armed rebellion over power and gain. 'Because of' is doing all the work of the match.

The candidate is right and the verse is wrong. “obtain the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 11:21, and Ether 11:18 is in fact its closest match in sense — an outsider with no claim overthrows a reigning king and takes the throne, which is what Daniel's 'vile person' does. But the phrase enters the Book of Mormon at Ether 11:10 and is used at 11:11 and 11:16 before it reaches here, and ADJUDICATING §4 asks for the adjudication at first use. The link is written at 11:10 with 11:11, 11:16, 11:18 and 13:24 in its recurrenceRefs, and it argues there that the chapter takes the phrase on a lawful succession and arrives at Daniel's sense by this verse. A reader who found the parallel here should read the row at 11:10.

“great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and the 1830 text preserves the KJV's double-l spelling that the 1920 edition modernised to 'marvelous' — so the temptation is real and CONVENTIONS §8 would ordinarily make something of it. But 'great and marvellous things' is a Book of Mormon formula long before Ether 11:20: it stands at 1 Nephi 1:14, Alma 9:6, 3 Nephi 17:16-17, Mormon 8:34 and, within this book, at Ether 4:15, where the catalogue adjudicates the sentence to 2 Corinthians 3:13-16 and Matthew 13:35. Ether 12:5 uses it again five verses after this chapter closes. A phrase the abridger has adopted as his own is not a fresh borrowing on each outing, and the Revelation 15 material that is adjudicated in this catalogue — the six-word run at 1 Nephi 1:14 — is a different phrase from a different clause of the verse. Cross-reference only: see Ether 4:15.

“to possess the land” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses — Deuteronomy 11:31, Joshua 1:11, Joshua 18:3, Judges 2:6, Judges 18:9, Nehemiah 9:15 and Amos 2:10 — and it is the standing Deuteronomic idiom for entering Canaan, used by the Book of Mormon throughout its own land-covenant material. No one of the seven is identifiable as the source. The distinctive content of Ether 11:21 is not the possession but the manner of it, 'after the manner which he brought their fathers', which is adjudicated to Amos 9:7.
